conflicts.note: The patent record is unambiguously Rolex (Zibach), but the engineering priority is contested. Perezcope's 2020 and 2025 articles disagree with each other in tone: the 2020 piece doubts Doxa's claims; the 2025 piece, citing newly surfaced Swiss press, argues Doxa was effectively first to a working valve.
positions: Rolex narrative: T. Walker Lloyd brought Bob Barth's idea to Rolex; Rolex filed CH492246 on 6 Nov 1967 (inventor André Zibach), granted 15 Jun 1970, and the Sea-Dweller followed.
Doxa narrative: Doxa co-developed the valve, tested it via Claude Wesly and introduced the Sub 300 T Conquistador in 1969 — shared patent claim per Urs Eschle.

Perezcope's 2025 evidence: a working Doxa prototype was demonstrably tested during Comex 'Ludion 2' (15 Nov 1967), just nine days after Rolex's filing, suggesting Doxa was at least parallel and arguably ahead in practical execution.
conflicts.topic: Who invented the helium release valve

conflicts.note: All sources agree the question is unsettled in Rolex's own archives; the 'lower-number-first' theory is presented as plausible folklore, not documented fact.
positions: Monochrome and Hodinkee treat the 6204 as the first reference to carry 'Submariner' on the dial (II.53-stamped cases), with the 6200 appearing later despite its lower number.

Rolex Passion Market and Rolex Magazine entertain the view that the 6200 was developed first as the Big-Crown 200m Sub but held back by Wilsdorf as too aggressive for retailers, with the slimmer 6204 launched in its place.

conflicts.note: The premium is real, but Fratello pushes back on the assumption that 'Red' equals 'rare' — condition and dial Mk are the more meaningful axes.
positions: Common framing: Red 1680s are the prized early variant, with premiums over white-text 1680s (Hodinkee, Fratello, Monochrome).
Fratello's vintage round-up: the 1680 was produced for most of its run with red text; total 1680 production was over 110,000, so Red Subs aren't truly rare in absolute terms.

conflicts.note: No source ranks these laterally as a hierarchy — the consensus is they are sibling watches with different priorities.
positions: Wind Vintage: explicitly refuses to call the 5512 superior, arguing condition trumps reference and that a great 5513 beats a poor 5512.
Hodinkee/Fratello: noted preference among some collectors for the 5513's two-line dial and lateral parity with the 5512 on everything but the movement.
Monochrome: frames the 5512 as the 'premium' option of the two at the time of sale, owing to its chronometer certification.

consensus.claim: The Submariner was developed in the early 1950s and publicly launched at the 1954 Basel Fair, with Rolex internally dating first production to 1953.
René-Paul Jeanneret, a Rolex director and diver close to Jacques Cousteau, was the internal champion who pushed Rolex to make a sporty yet wearable waterproof watch.
The first Submariner was marketed as waterproof to 100m, narrowly bettering Blancpain's Fifty Fathoms (rated to ~91m), which had appeared months earlier in 1953.
Crown guards arrived with the 5512 in 1959; it was the first Rolex of any kind to use them.

The 5512 and 5513 share the same case and design; the defining difference is that the 5512 carried a chronometer-certified movement (after early non-chronometer 5512s using cal. 1530), while the 5513 used non-chronometer calibres 1530 and later 1520.
5512 production ran roughly 1959–1980; 5513 production ran roughly 1962–1989, making the 5513 one of Rolex's longest continuously produced sports watch references.
Rolex produced roughly one 5512 for every ten 5513s — about 17,338 vs. 151,449 according to figures cited in Rolex's 2024 Submariner publication.
The 5513 dial evolved through three broad eras: glossy gilt (c.1962–67), matte (c.1967–84), and glossy black with white-gold-surround applied markers (c.1984–89).

Within matte-dial 5513s, collectors classify a sequence from Meters First → Non-Serif/Serif → Pre-COMEX → Maxi I–V, distinguished by depth-rating placement, serifs on the 'f' of 'ft', the shape of the coronet, position of the '=' sign, and the size of the tritium plots.
The 1680, introduced in 1969, was the first Submariner with a date and cyclops; early examples with 'Submariner' in red are nicknamed the 'Red Sub'.
In 1969 Rolex also released the first solid 18k yellow gold Submariner (1680/8), available with black or blue dial/bezel, marking the model's expansion beyond pure tool watch.
Rolex produced 5513s (and the helium-valve-equipped 5514) for COMEX from the early 1970s; some 5513s were also retrofitted with prototype gas-escape valves before the dedicated 5514 existed.
The MilSub (5513, and later the dedicated 5517) was made for the British MoD with fixed bar lugs, sword hands, an encircled 'T' on the dial, and a fully graduated 60-minute bezel.
The Submariner is foundational to the Bond visual identity: a 6538 (Big Crown) on Sean Connery in Dr. No, From Russia with Love and Goldfinger, and a 5513 worn by Roger Moore in Live and Let Die.
The 5508 was the last Submariner produced without crown guards and the first to use tritium rather than radium lume.
The 5513's late-life transition (c.1984) to a glossy black dial with white-gold-surround applied markers established the visual template carried into the five-digit 14060 and beyond.

marks.name: Meters First (5513 matte)

marks.explanation: From c.1969 the depth rating order switched to '660ft=200m'; this is the matte-dial form most commonly encountered through to ~1982.
marks.name: Feet First (5513 matte)

marks.explanation: Mid-matte 5513 dials introduced around late 1969 / early 1970 (early 2.0 mil serials), distinguished by the presence or absence of serifs on the depth-rating typography.

model_context: The Rolex Submariner sits at the centre of the brand's professional/tool-watch identity. Conceived in the early 1950s under the influence of board member René-Paul Jeanneret — a diving enthusiast close to Jacques Cousteau — it was Rolex's deliberate move into purpose-built sports watches, alongside the Explorer and Turn-O-Graph. The Submariner was launched at the 1954 Basel Fair (Rolex internally dates production to 1953), debuting as the first wristwatch publicly rated to 100m. From the 6204/6205/6200 'pre-crown-guard' era through the Big Crown 6536/6538/5510/5508, Rolex iterated rapidly: bigger crowns, deeper ratings (200m by the 6200), the Mercedes hand, tritium lume (from 5508), and finally crown guards in 1959 with the 5512. The 5512 (1959–1980) and 5513 (1962–1989) define the long crown-guard, no-date, four-digit core: the 5512 is the chronometer-certified watch (calibres 1530/1560/1570), the 5513 the non-chronometer sibling (1530/1520) introduced as a more accessible variant. The 5513's near-three-decade run made it Rolex's everyman dive watch and the reference under which most special-purpose variants were issued (MilSub 5513, COMEX, Explorer-dial, the 'Shadow' South African pieces). The date arrived in 1969 with the 1680, prompted in part by the Sea-Dweller's 1967 introduction; the 1680 was also the first gold Submariner. Demand was driven by post-war recreational diving (Cousteau, the Aqua-Lung), military and commercial-dive contracts (Royal Navy, COMEX), and a steady drumbeat of cultural placement — most famously Sean Connery's 6538 in Dr. No and later Roger Moore's modified 5513 in Live and Let Die. The Submariner is widely regarded as the template the rest of the dive-watch industry followed.

module_candidates.rationale: Distinct MoD specification (sword hands, fixed lugs, circled-T, fully graduated bezel), well-defined production window mid-1970s, and a clear lateral relationship to 'The Shadow' and other military-issue pieces.
COMEX partnership from c.1970 produced a discrete family of dials and case modifications (HEVs on 5513/5514, no HEV on 1680), plus its own provenance ecosystem worth a dedicated page.
The 1967 Sea-Dweller is the direct trigger for the 1680 date Sub; the Single Red / Double Red lineage and the gas-escape-valve story (including the Doxa controversy) deserve their own treatment.
Mk I–VI (plus service Mk VII) dial taxonomy, meters-first vs feet-first, and the watershed introduction of the date make this a self-contained module.
VRFM's dedicated gold-Sub article shows the depth of variation (nipple dials, tropical blues, alloy evolution) — distinct enough from the steel core to warrant separation.
6538 (Connery), 5513 (Moore), and the documented screen-used props at Phillips/Christie's are a cohesive cultural module that otherwise risks dominating the main 5512/5513 narrative.
The 1953–1959 era has enough internal variation (Big Crown vs small crown, Explorer dials, OCC vs non-chronometer, radium → tritium transition with the 5508) to merit its own anchor page.
5513mattedial.com alone is a dense reference that doesn't fit neatly inside a model-line overview; ideal as a dedicated identification module.

module_candidates.module: Submariner peer set (Fifty Fathoms, Seamaster 300, Doxa Sub 300, Tudor Submariner, Ploprof)
module_candidates.rationale: Treating these laterally — not as alternatives 'beneath' the Sub — gives readers genre context; Watchfinder and Fratello provide a ready starting list.
The bridge from the 5513's late glossy dial to the modern 41mm Sub is a coherent story (sapphire, unidirectional bezel, 904L, ceramic) and is explicitly excluded by Hodinkee's Reference Points.

stories.title: Auguste Piccard's 1953 Bathyscaphe dive
stories.why: The 3,131.8m dive of the Bathyscaphe Trieste with a Rolex Deep Sea prototype attached set the public-relations stage for the Submariner's launch and seeded Rolex's deep-sea marketing posture.

stories.title: Jacques Cousteau testing 1953 prototype Submariners
stories.why: Rolex Magazine surfaces a letter and photograph showing Cousteau wearing a Submariner prototype in 1953 — direct evidence of the Cousteau/Jeanneret link that drove the model's design brief.

stories.title: Roger Moore's buzz-saw / magnetic 5513 in Live and Let Die
stories.why: The Phillips and Christie's lot essays document the actual screen-used 5513 prop — Syd Cain–designed gadget watch, caseback engraved 'Roger Moore 007' — anchoring the 5513's place in Bond lore beyond styling.

stories.title: 'The Shadow' — South African Special Forces 5513
stories.why: A 1975 factory-blacked-out 5513 confirmed by Rolex Patrimoine, made for Operation Savannah; Marcello Pisani called it 'the only watch I will ever regret', and it seeded the entire later genre of PVD-coated Bamford/Pro Hunter pieces.

stories.title: COMEX diver Stuart L.'s prototype-HEV 5513
stories.why: A 1971 (2.8-mil) 5513 retrofitted with a prototype gas-escape valve, traced directly to a former Royal Navy / COMEX commercial diver who sent it back to Rolex periodically for updates — rare first-hand provenance for the COMEX programme.

stories.title: Dr. Ralph W. Brauer's Single Red Sea-Dweller
stories.why: The very first Sea-Dweller fitted with a gas-escape valve, used in Comex 'Physalie'/'Hydra' tests; the watch later turned up under the late professor's mattress with cash and a handgun — a useful reminder of how close the early valve story sits to the 5513/Sub family.

stories.title: Doxa's 'Ludion 2' valve test, 15 Nov 1967
stories.why: Newly surfaced 1968 Swiss press reporting on Claude Wesly's helium-valve Doxa Sub 300 prototype — nine days after Rolex filed its patent — complicates the tidy 'Rolex invented it' narrative used in many Submariner histories.

stories.title: Chuck Yeager's 6538 in 1956
stories.why: Rolex Magazine surfaces a 1956 photograph of test pilot Chuck Yeager wearing a Big Crown 6538 — a vivid early example of the Submariner crossing from divers to other 'achievers'.

stories.title: Elvis Presley's Big Crown Submariner
stories.why: A 1962 photograph of Elvis with a Big Crown Sub places the model in early rock-and-roll iconography, well before the 'Bond' overlay hardened.

stories.title: Brian Kelly's Submariner in Flipper
stories.why: Television placement on Porter Ricks in Flipper — an under-discussed thread of the Submariner's early-1960s mainstream presence in family TV alongside its Bond appearances.

stories.title: Mercedes Gleitze and the 1927 Channel swim
stories.why: Pre-Submariner, but the founding act of Rolex's diver-credibility narrative — a Rolex Oyster around Gleitze's neck during her Channel attempt set the template for everything the Submariner later built on.

stories.title: Tom Place's lost 1996 Submariner
stories.why: Fratello reader/stuntman Tom Place still dives the lake where he lost his Sub — a contemporary human story illustrating the watch's grip on its owners decades after manufacture.

stories.title: Harold Holt's two Submariners
stories.why: Rolex provided the late Australian PM Harold Holt — a keen skin diver — with two Submariners; Holt disappeared on an ocean swim in December 1967, an unusually sombre chapter in the model's cultural history.
